title: Get a microwave's glass tray back onto its drive coupler
instruction: The microwave's glass tray wobbles. Get it sitting properly on its drive so it will turn, then let go.
context: Nearly every household microwave has a removable glass turntable that people take out and wash. Panasonic's manual says not to run the oven unless the glass tray is fully engaged on the drive hub, and its troubleshooting table lists "the glass tray wobbles" as a fault. A tray resting on top of the coupler's lobes rocks, can stall, and lets dishes slide. The hub and lobes sit under a 34 cm tray, so they cannot be seen while you line them up, and the tray clears the side walls by only 7.5 mm on each side.
real_product: Panasonic NN-SN686S, 1.2 cu ft, 1200 W. Source: the Panasonic operating manual F0003BT30AP (help.panasonic.ca/PCS/OperatingInstructions/nn-sn686_en_om.pdf, downloaded and read). It gives the cavity as 355 W x 251 H x 365 D mm, the outside as 525 x 310 x 401 mm and the weight as 11.5 kg. Parts listed: glass tray F06015Q00AP and roller ring assembly F290D6W50XP. Retail and spec listings give the turntable as 13.4 in (340 mm). Manual text: "DO NOT operate the oven without the Glass Tray fully engaged on the drive hub... Verify that the Glass Tray is properly engaged and rotating by observing its rotation when you press Start." Troubleshooting: "The Glass Tray wobbles: The Glass Tray is not positioned properly on the Roller Ring... reset Roller Ring and Glass Tray properly." No source found for the coupler's lobe shape, its height, or the recess depth under the tray; these would be estimates or need measuring on a real part. Does the product remove the fault? Not entirely: the manual itself documents the wobble. But the manual's own check is to press Start and watch the tray, and a motor-driven coupler turning under a tray that rides on it may slip until the lobes drop into the recesses by themselves. That undercuts the claim that running the oven leaves the tray riding, and I could not confirm what this model does. The bigger problem is that the forced skill is not distinct: the ordinary reinstall after washing already means setting the tray down and turning it until it drops. T
fault: After washing, the tray was set back with its underside hub resting on top of the three coupler lobes instead of over them. The tray sits about 5 mm high in the middle, rocks on the roller ring, and will not be driven.
skill: Working inside the cavity from its front edge, which is all that is reachable, keep light downward pressure on the tray and turn it in short strokes until its recesses drop over the lobes, by feel because the lobes are hidden. This is the same skill as the ordinary reinstall, and the same family as accepted #893 (find rotational phase by contact while seating). In this robot's reach it is one arm ratcheting the front rim sideways a few centimetres at a time.

reviewer_reasons:
wide-funnel deepen, 17 Nov: killed. 1) Importance, duplicate: it is the same rotational phase-by-contact seating as accepted #893; #719 and #1890 were closed for good as its duplicates. It also nearly duplicates #2475, another team's pending stand-mixer bowl with three hidden bumps turned by feel until it drops, and that team holds the idea.
2) The recovery is the ordinary job. Reinstalling a washed tray already means setting it down and turning it until it drops, so the "fault" is just that job unfinished (our #2400 objection). The roller-ring half of the fault can only be fixed by taking the tray out and reinstalling it, which is ordinary again.
3) The difficulty is too low (#2127 precedent): one arm, a few sideways drags of a few centimetres under light pressure.
4) Construct validity: Panasonic's own check is to press Start, and a turning coupler may seat a riding tray by itself, so the claim that "ordinary fails" is unverified for this model. The lobe and recess geometry has no published source.
5) Assets: SimReady has no microwave. The recognizable appliance would be built from primitives plus custom tray, coupler and ring meshes, which risks an "egregious simplification" flag.
6) Feasibility: top-down grips reach only the front 2 cm of the cavity (the wrist hits the oven top beyond that). The open door blocks the left arm, so the task is one-armed and loses the two-hand rationale. Uniform 1.2 friction on a ring that should roll makes turning the tray stiff unless the ring is jointed.
7) Scoring has no real intermediate state, so partial credit is thin.
Not worth a day's build.
